content: Norovirus is the causative agent responsible for norovirus infection. These viruses belong to the genus Norovirus and are a group of related, single-stranded RNA viruses that lack an envelope. They are known to cause acute gastroenteritis in humans. Noroviruses are classified under the family Caliciviridae. Common Causes of Norovirus Transmission Norovirus is primarily transmitted through person-to-person contact, as well as through contaminated food and water. The majority of cases are attributed to contact transmission, while a significant proportion is foodborne. Strains belonging to genogroup GI are more frequently transmitted via water due to their enhanced stability in aquatic environments compared to other strains of the virus. Globally, norovirus ranks among the leading causes of foodborne viral infections. Transmission can occur at various stages of food production, both preand post-harvest. For example, shellfish may become contaminated through exposure to fecal matter in water, while fresh and frozen berries can be tainted by sewage-contaminated water or through direct contact during harvesting. Foodborne viral outbreaks often involve a mixture of viral strains, which increases the risk of genetic recombination. Research indicates that approximately 7% of foodborne outbreaks can be traced back to a common source. Less Common Causes of Norovirus Transmission Norovirus can also spread in healthcare settings, leading to nosocomial infections that place a significant burden on healthcare systems. Immunocompromised individuals are particularly vulnerable, as chronic infections in these patients can result in the emergence of numerous norovirus variants. This intra-host viral variation may give rise to novel strains that differ significantly from those involved in previous outbreaks, potentially evading herd immunity. To date, there is no evidence that animal norovirus strains can infect humans. However, intra-species transmission has been documented. Human norovirus has been detected in the feces of pigs, cattle, and dogs, suggesting potential cross-species interactions, though the implications for human health remain unclear.
